subject: Wheel A drawn as a surveyed plot in one-bit ink, a dithered web with each tooth a numbered lot whose flat tone says whether it meshes and a 2 px traverse run out to the lot at the mesh station, beside two survey glyphs: a two-row scale bar for the ratio and a stepped section profile for the scale.
controls: ratio: the scale bar's two rows re-divide into the ratio's two numbers (3 over 2 at 3:2, 1 over 1 at 1:1, 3 over 1 at 3:1) in alternating black and white blocks (shape of the glyph).
teeth: the plot's outline redraws with 3 to 16 lots, renumbered round the boundary (shape of the hero).
mesh: lots whose teeth slip pull their tips in to the root circle and drop from their 50 % tone to black, evenly round the wheel (shape, with tone as the second cue).
scale: the section profile's steps re-rise by the scale's intervals (shape of the glyph).
risks: Stretch, and I'd say plainly it doesn't fit. The case for it: a gear is already a flat, chunky, plan-view object, so one-bit ink needs none of the figurative anatomy that sank toro's bull. Against: a lone cog in a 2 px white outline is the settings icon, which craft.md bans outright; only wheel A is drawn, so the mesh between two wheels, the machine's whole rule, is off screen and the ratio is demoted to a glyph; every outline is #CDCDCD, so there's no one brightest element; dither can't move (the web is static run-length rects, ~600 at 2 px, and the lots are flat greys standing in for dither); the survey language (lots, traverse, scale bar, section) is labels on a cog, not a plan of anything. Muted: the lots go black and the traverse hides.
